body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: I have yet seen Mr. Terry but twice, in the Iron Chest as Sir Edward Mortimer, and in the farce of Blue Devils as Megrim, characters perhaps not the most favourable for an appreciation of his talents, for there is more noise and violence in Mr. Colman's tragedy heroes than any thing else, and Megrim, the hypochondriac, is rather the cause of humour in others than humorous in himself. There is quite sufficient however in these two appearances to give one a high idea of Mr. Terry's abilities; though some other pieces for which he is announced at the time I am writing, will enable me to form a more complete judgment of him on a future occasion.

The aspect of this gentleman is of a very serious cast; his figure is spare, and not striking; his eyes rather too much inclining to be shut, but capable of a calm penetration; his other features marked, particularly about the mouth, the muscles of which have a strong and liny cut like those of Mr. Young. What is very rare on the stage, and tends to recommend a new performer at once to its frequenters, is the originality which Mr. Terry evinces in parts that have been played by numbers. Some persons compare him with Mr. Kemble, others with Mr. Young, and by others he is said to imitate both; but people in general are extremely apt to confound all the shades of a grave style with each other, and to class them under one particular colour on which they have been accustomed to look. Mr. Terry has quite a ground of his own to stand upon, and promises to maintain it well. The best Mortimer that has lately been seen is Elliston's; but unluckily it is a character containing much temptation to rant; and though many individual touches of his performance are excellent, there is a general robustness, if I may so call it, in his grief, which overcomes the finer and more languid nature of Sir Edward's misery, the principal feature of which is an exhausted despair. Mr. Terry preserves this better, I think, than Mr. Elliston, and as his delivery is of a more fluent and natural cast, his performance altogether has a less artificial effect, and takes us more along with it into the recesses of its grief. His final scene, it must be confessed, is sufficiently outrageous, but then it is intended by the author for the madness of impatience, and the superiority of his calmer moments over those of Elliston appear to me to be particularly discernible during the trial of Wilford, when by side hints and gestures he warns his intended victim not to forget the oath of secresy to which he had bound himself. They deviated into no theatrical starings or eye-rollings; but made their solemn appeal in an earnest though rather languid manner, which seemed to indulge the natural weariness of his sorrow in the security with which he relied on the youth's honour.

The appearance of Mr. Terry in Blue Devils, though a farce, is not so great a departure from tragedy as may seem at first sight, for James Megrim is a very serious personage after all; and no notion of the actor's humour is to be gathered from the part, at all resembling what will be obtained from his performance, for instance, of Sir Anthony Absolute in the Rivals. Still such a character is not without its pleasantry, in enabling the actor to shew us that he feels how far its seriousness should go in order to have a ridiculous effect; and Mr. Terry did this most successfully, coming here again into advantageous comparison with Elliston, whose effect though greater, because the dryness of his humour is more prominent, is less natural on that account, since it tends to confound the feelings of the character with those of the spectators. Elliston is inimitable where his dry humour is proper, as in the Duke Aranza for instance, which is a character that enjoys its own pleasantry; nor is there an actor who can better relish the humour of Megrim; but this relish, unless well concealed, may be fatal to the propriety of a performance, as is particularly the case with Munden, who never can help grinning at the dryness he puts on and playing the bye-stander to his own exploits. It is in avoiding this tempting fault, that the original excellence of Mr. Terry's Megrim consists. What appears indeed to be the principal feature of his style, as far as I can judge of it hitherto, is a strong love of simplicity and natural fitness, not avoiding what may be passionate provided it be true, but studiously setting his face against every thing out of character. By the way, the farce of Blue Devils is not only a very amusing one, but involves a useful piece of instruction. It is the story of an English hypochondriac, who during his travels in France, is every day on the point of shooting himself, and is only prevented from terminating his wearisome existence by suddenly tasting the pleasures of a benevolent action, which chance throws in his way to perform. This is a very good lesson: but after all, it is only half a one. A hypochondriac's miseries generally arise from a mixed cause of body as well as mind; and it is not doing enough for him, unless his animal as well as intellectual spirits are set a going: Good actions are the best recipe for the latter, but without a recipe for the former also, the nerves will continually interrupt the enjoyment. We should have a farce then, if possible, to shew us a man debauching himself into the Blue Devils, eating, and drinking, and nocturnalizing himself into bad nerves, and then recovering himself by means of temperance and regular hours. Without these, even good actions will not make us happy; but with good actions and these together, we may defy all sorts of devils, blue, black, and scarlet.
